rows.subtopic: A conflict between two team members
rows.subtype: Approach: listening separately to each side first [Action]
rows.description: A lead meets two colleagues one at a time, asking what happened and what each needs. Both feel heard, and she learns the fight began over unclear ownership of a release task.

rows.subtopic: A conflict between two team members
rows.subtype: Approach: root cause analysis with five whys [Thinking]
rows.description: Asking why repeatedly, the lead finds the quarrel is not about personality. Overlapping task assignments and a missing handover note keep creating blame between the two.

rows.subtopic: A conflict between two team members
rows.subtype: Approach: hoping it fades without intervention [Pitfall]
rows.description: Wanting to avoid awkwardness, the lead ignores sharp comments in meetings. The tension spreads, others pick sides, and one member starts looking for another job.

rows.subtopic: A conflict between two team members
rows.subtype: Approach: escalating to HR for a serious conduct issue [Revision]
rows.description: When one complaint involves demeaning remarks rather than a task dispute, the lead sees that mediation is not enough. She documents facts and brings in HR, following company process.

rows.subtopic: Saving from allowance
rows.subtype: Approach: setting a goal with an amount and date [Thinking]
rows.description: A teen wants a secondhand bicycle costing 4,000 rupees in six months, divides it into a weekly saving figure, and finds it is more realistic than he thought.

rows.subtopic: Saving from allowance
rows.subtype: Approach: splitting money into save, spend and give [Thinking]
rows.description: A teen decides that half goes to the goal, a third to spending and the rest to family gifts or charity, which balances her wants and values so the plan feels fair.

rows.subtopic: Saving from allowance
rows.subtype: Approach: spending impulsively at the first temptation [Pitfall]
rows.description: A teen with saved money sees a sale online and buys a pair of shoes on impulse, then finds that the bicycle goal is set back by two months.

rows.subtopic: Saving from allowance
rows.subtype: Approach: adjusting the goal after a shortfall [Revision]
rows.description: After a month with unexpected school expenses, a student extends the target date by four weeks and lowers the weekly amount rather than abandoning the plan altogether.

rows.subtopic: Preparing for a science or robotics competition
rows.subtype: Approach: reading the rules and working backward from the deadline [Thinking]
rows.description: A team reads the competition rules and dates, then counts backward from the event to set milestones for design, build, testing and rehearsal, leaving a final week free.

rows.subtopic: Preparing for a science or robotics competition
rows.subtype: Approach: brainstorming many ideas then selecting one [Thinking]
rows.description: Team members write twenty possible robot designs on sticky notes without judging, then vote using cost, time and skill criteria, and choose a simple line-follower with a clever sensor arrangement.

rows.subtopic: Preparing for a science or robotics competition
rows.subtype: Approach: last-minute changes before the event [Pitfall]
rows.description: The night before, the team rewrites the control code to add a new feature, never tests it fully, and the robot misbehaves in the first round, showing the risk of untested changes.

rows.subtopic: Preparing for a science or robotics competition
rows.subtype: Approach: reviewing the result and learning from the loss [Revision]
rows.description: After finishing fifth, the team meets, lists what went well and what failed, such as poor calibration, and writes changes for the next year, treating the result as feedback rather than a verdict.

rows.subtopic: Earning a reward
rows.subtype: Approach: simple step list [Action]
rows.description: A child follows the sticker chart: brush teeth, finish milk, put shoes in the rack. Each finished task gets a sticker, and ten stickers means a trip to the park.

rows.subtopic: Earning a reward
rows.subtype: Approach: bargaining [Action]
rows.description: A child says, "If I eat all my vegetables, can I have two stories tonight?" Naming the price and the prize makes the deal explicit.

rows.subtopic: Earning a reward
rows.subtype: Approach: magical thinking [Pitfall]
rows.description: A child wishes on the first star for extra stickers and expects them to show up on the chart in the morning. The wish is trusted more than the routine.

rows.subtopic: Earning a reward
rows.subtype: Approach: asking an adult [Revision]
rows.description: Unsure how far off the reward is, a child asks mother, "How many more stickers?" She counts three with the child, and the goal becomes something concrete.

rows.subtopic: Reaching a fitness or sports goal
rows.subtype: Approach: setting a specific measurable target [Thinking]
rows.description: A teen wants to run 5 km without stopping for a school race, so she writes the date, a starting distance of one kilometre, and a plan to add a little each week.

rows.subtopic: Reaching a fitness or sports goal
rows.subtype: Approach: progressive plan with rest days [Action]
rows.description: A student follows a run and walk schedule three days a week with rest between, records each session in a diary, and increases distance slowly to avoid overuse pain.

rows.subtopic: Reaching a fitness or sports goal
rows.subtype: Approach: doing too much too soon [Pitfall]
rows.description: A teen aiming for the school team trains twice daily from day one, ignores soreness, and picks up a strain that keeps him out for weeks, delaying the goal he wanted to speed up.

rows.subtopic: Reaching a fitness or sports goal
rows.subtype: Approach: listening to the body and adapting [Revision]
rows.description: Noticing knee pain after running on hard roads, a teen cuts distance, switches to a softer field, asks the coach about shoes, and returns to the plan gradually.

rows.subtopic: Deciding whether to whistleblow
rows.subtype: Approach: gather facts before judging [Thinking]
rows.description: A junior auditor notices invoices repeatedly paid to a vendor with no delivery record. Before concluding anything, the auditor asks what other explanations exist and what evidence would separate error from wrongdoing.

rows.subtopic: Deciding whether to whistleblow
rows.subtype: Approach: check the company whistleblower policy and legal protection [Action]
rows.description: The auditor reads the internal policy and the general protections available in law, and considers who receives a report and how confidentiality is kept. Knowing the channels avoids acting in a way that exposes the person needlessly.

rows.subtopic: Deciding whether to whistleblow
rows.subtype: Approach: confront the colleague in anger [Pitfall]
rows.description: Upset by what was found, the person accuses the colleague in an open office. The colleague deletes files and the team turns hostile, and the chance of a calm, documented process is lost.

rows.subtopic: Deciding whether to whistleblow
rows.subtype: Approach: follow up and escalate when nothing happens [Revision]
rows.description: After weeks without a response, the auditor asks compliance for an acknowledgement and, if still ignored, considers an external regulator with advice from a lawyer. Persistence through lawful channels keeps the issue alive.
